questions.question: What bound structure and observational consequence anchor the paper's future 'island universe' scenario?

options.A: The Local Group remains bound, while more distant structures fade beyond the de Sitter horizon on roughly a 100-billion-year timescale
options.B: The Virgo cluster remains bound, while the Local Group crosses the horizon within 10 billion years
options.C: The Milky Way becomes unbound, exposing an increasingly dense Hubble flow
options.D: All galaxies merge before dark energy dominates, leaving a measurable external redshift field

questions.rationale: The authors argue distant galaxies become invisible while the merger product of the Local Group remains observable.
questions.evidence_quote: Both analytic [7] and numerical [10] calculations indicate that the Local Group remains gravitationally bound

questions.question: Why would future observers not infer dark energy from the matter-to-vacuum ratio inside their horizon volume?

options.A: The ratio may reach ρM/ρΛ∼10⁻¹², but local bound-system observations probe no scales where Λ dominates dynamics
options.B: Vacuum energy decays to exactly zero inside gravitationally bound systems
options.C: Dark energy becomes matter-like and is confused with baryons
options.D: The ratio remains near unity, making its effect impossible to separate from dark matter

questions.rationale: Extreme vacuum-energy dominance does not help if observers lack probes of relevant length scales.
questions.evidence_quote: they will have no probes of the length scales over which Λ dominates gravitational dynamics

questions.question: At about 100 Gyr, how does the paper characterize the CMB peak and its intensity?

options.A: Peak wavelength near 1 m (about 300 MHz), with intensity dimmed by roughly 12 orders of magnitude
options.B: Peak wavelength near 3×10⁷ cm (1 kHz), with intensity unchanged
options.C: Peak wavelength near 1 μm, with intensity increased by 12 orders of magnitude
options.D: Peak wavelength beyond the horizon already, with no finite-frequency description

questions.rationale: The CMB is redshifted to radio wavelengths and dramatically diluted before becoming fully inaccessible.
questions.evidence_quote: At t ≈100 Gyr, the peak wavelength of the cosmic microwave background will be redshifted to roughly λ ≈1 m, or a frequency of roughly 300 MHz.

questions.question: What local-medium effect does the paper identify as screening the CMB before its peak wavelength exceeds the horizon?

options.A: The redshifted peak falls below the interstellar plasma frequency, estimated near 1 kHz for ne≈0.03 cm⁻³
options.B: Dust grains absorb it at the 300-MHz peak because of a 3-K resonance
options.C: The stellar radiation field ionizes the CMB photons above 1 GHz
options.D: The Galactic magnetic field reflects all wavelengths longer than 1 m

questions.rationale: The cited pulsar-dispersion electron density gives a plasma cutoff that blocks radio propagation.
questions.evidence_quote: the microwave background peak will redshift below the plasma frequency of the interstellar medium

questions.question: Why does general relativity alone not force future observers to posit a Big Bang?

options.A: The expansion inference depends on homogeneity and isotropy, which their isolated, apparently empty surroundings will not satisfy
options.B: General relativity predicts static solutions only when Λ is zero
options.C: Planetary tests will establish that gravity is Newtonian at cosmological scales
options.D: A bound galaxy has no finite future under Einstein's equations

questions.rationale: Without the cosmological hypothesis, an isolated gravitating system in an otherwise empty static region is consistent with GR.
questions.evidence_quote: The inference that the universe must be expanding or contracting is dependent upon the cosmological hypothesis that we live in an isotropic and homogeneous universe.

questions.question: What change to helium abundance does the paper project after about 100 Gyr, and why does it weaken evidence for primordial nucleosynthesis?

options.A: Stellar processing may drive helium mass fraction toward Y=0.6, dwarfing primordial Y=0.25
options.B: Helium falls toward Y=0.025, making stellar contamination negligible
options.C: Primordial helium rises to Y=0.6 while stellar helium remains 0.25
options.D: Helium remains Y=0.25, but deuterium rises to 0.6

questions.rationale: Future stellar processing would contaminate helium and destroy much of the deuterium relic signal.
questions.evidence_quote: the ultimate extrapolation of light elemental abundances, following many generations of stellar evolution, is a mass fraction of helium given by Y = 0.6

questions.question: Which specific observational route to primordial deuterium would be lost along with distant cosmological tracers?

options.A: Lyman-α absorption by intergalactic systems back-lit by quasars
options.B: Deuterium emission from the Local Group's oldest stars
options.C: Radio absorption against the cosmic infrared background
options.D: Stellar parallax of nearby white dwarfs

questions.rationale: Both the background quasars and absorbing systems eventually redshift outside the horizon.
questions.evidence_quote: both the QSOs and the Lyman-α systems will have redshifted outside of the horizon

questions.question: What two-sided age constraints do the authors think future astronomers could still derive for their local system?

options.A: A lower bound from the oldest stars and an upper bound from the time needed to synthesize observed helium
options.B: A lower bound from CMB anisotropies and an upper bound from the Hubble constant
options.C: A lower bound from primordial deuterium and an upper bound from quasar absorption
options.D: A lower bound from galaxy counts and an upper bound from distant supernovae

questions.rationale: Local stellar evolution remains available even if cosmological relic abundance evidence disappears.
questions.evidence_quote: They will be able to examine the locus of all stars and extrapolate to the oldest such stars to estimate a lower bound on the age of the galaxy.

questions.question: How does the paper distinguish the near-future and far-future ability to detect dark energy?

options.A: An epoch an order of magnitude younger lacked detectable dark-energy effects; one an order older loses evidence of expansion itself
options.B: Both younger and older observers detect dark energy from the CMB with equal ease
options.C: Younger observers see accelerated expansion, but older observers infer it from local galaxy motion
options.D: Only observers before matter-radiation equality can detect dark energy

questions.rationale: The authors frame the present as a narrow observational window, bracketed by eras unable to establish Λ's role.
questions.evidence_quote: Observers when the universe was an order of magnitude younger would not have been able to discern any effects of dark energy on the expansion

questions.question: What does the paper mean by the future 'return of a static universe'?

options.A: The locally visible universe will consist of a bound island with no observable Hubble flow, not a globally non-expanding cosmos
options.B: The global scale factor will reverse and contract to a static radius
options.C: Dark energy will vanish, leaving a homogeneous static universe everywhere
options.D: All matter will become stationary relative to the de Sitter horizon

questions.rationale: The apparent static picture is an observational limitation from the bound island and horizon, while global de Sitter expansion continues.
questions.evidence_quote: the static version of de Sitter space outside of that system will eventually become the appropriate physical coordinate system
